4:6.text: Thus wast thou decked with gold and silver; and thy raiment was of fine linen, and silk, and broidered work; thou didst eat fine flour, and honey, and oil: and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom.

provenance.other: “silk” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Proverbs 31:22, Ezekiel 16:10, Ezekiel 16:13 and Revelation 18:12 — and only two of them set it beside fine linen and beside gold and silver: Ezekiel 16:13 and Revelation 18:12. “fine twined linen” occurs in exactly twenty KJV verses, every one of them in Exodus and every one of them describing the tabernacle's hangings or the high priest's ephod. “costly apparel” occurs in no KJV verse at all; the nearest thing to it is 1 Timothy 2:9's “costly array”, in a list that likewise runs gold and pearls before the clothing.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 16 is the KJV's set piece on a people decked in gold and silver, fine linen and silk, who then 'trust in thine own beauty' (16:15) — and the same chapter itemizes the resulting sin at 16:49 as 'pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness ... neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.' Alma 4 works through that itemization in Ezekiel's own order: the finery at 4:6, the pride at 4:6 and 4:8, and the hand not strengthened at 4:12, where the needy have backs turned on them. Recover the context and the chapter is not merely denouncing luxury; it is running Ezekiel's indictment of Jerusalem against a church. The second borrowing cuts the other way: 'fine twined linen' is, in the KJV, sanctuary cloth and nothing else — the veil, the court hangings, the ephod — so the fabric Exodus reserves for the holy place and the high priest's vestment is here being worn as costly apparel by the congregation of a church whose high priest is Alma, who at 4:20 will confine himself wholly to the high priesthood.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 18:12's merchandise of Babylon has the same four commodities and is the likelier source if the writer is reaching for a picture of doomed commerce rather than of a decked bride.

4:6.note: 'Their exceeding riches, and their fine silks, and their fine twined linen, and ... their gold, and their silver, and all manner of precious things ... they began to wear very costly apparel.' The commodity list is Ezekiel 16:13's, which is the KJV's one verse pairing silk with fine linen under gold and silver. The chapter's argument is a reversal of Alma 1: at 1:32 costly apparel and the pride of the eyes belonged to those outside the church, and here the same wardrobe and the same phrase have moved inside it, 'even to exceed the pride of those who did not belong' (4:9). Adjudicated at Alma 1:29 and 1:32 as the book's first use; the row is given here because the transfer of the wardrobe is the point being made.

4:8.text: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.

provenance.other: “set not your heart upon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon's own form, 'set their hearts upon riches', occurs in no KJV verse; what it has done is turn the psalm's prohibition into a report that it was disobeyed.
provenance.significance: Alma 4:8 makes two charges in one clause — that the people were lifted up in the pride of their eyes, and that they set their hearts upon riches and upon the vain things of the world — and Psalm 62 makes exactly those two in consecutive verses. Verse 9 weighs the proud: 'men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.' Verse 10 forbids the riches: 'become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.' Vanity, riches and the setting of the heart are all three in the psalm's two verses and all three in Alma's one, which is more than the shared idiom by itself would give. The metalepsis is that the psalm is a psalm of trust — 'my soul, wait thou only upon God' — so the sin Alma names is, in its source, a failure of waiting.

4:8.note: 'To set their hearts upon riches and upon the vain things of the world.' Psalm 62:10 is the only KJV verse that puts the heart, the setting, and riches into one prohibition, and the surrounding words supply Alma's other term as well: the psalmist's 'become not vain' and 'lighter than vanity' stand behind 'the vain things of the world'. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion; the evidence is the coincidence of three elements, not the length of a run.

4:9.text: For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men?

provenance.other: “envying and strife” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 1 Corinthians 3:3, James 3:14 and James 3:16 — and only the first of them is addressed to a congregation about its own divisions. The plural 'envyings' of the Book of Mormon's wording is the form at 2 Corinthians 12:20 and Galatians 5:21, both of them Pauline vice lists.
provenance.significance: The verse that supplies the pair also supplies the diagnosis Alma 4 is reaching for and does not state: 'ye are yet carnal ... and walk as men.' Paul's charge at Corinth is not that the church has sinners in it but that its members behave like people who are not in it — which is precisely Alma 4:9's sting, that the pride within the church came 'even to exceed the pride of those who did not belong to the church of God.' The same three-verse cluster, at 1 Corinthians 3:3-4, is also one of only three KJV settings for “not carnal”; the third is 2 Corinthians 10:4, which stands behind this chapter's other Pauline reach, at 4:19.

4:9.note: 'There was envyings, and strife, and malice, and persecutions, and pride.' The head of the list is the KJV pair, and the setting is Paul's: divisions inside a congregation. Alma 1:32 had put envyings and strife outside the church, among those who did not belong to it; four chapters later the identical vocabulary describes the church itself, which is the reversal the whole chapter is built on. Recorded here rather than at Alma 1:32 because the second use is the argument.

4:10.text: But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.

provenance.other: “stumblingblock” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses. Nine of them are a stumblingblock laid by God, by an idol, or by an enemy; only 1 Corinthians 8:9 and Romans 14:13 have it laid inadvertently by the strong in the path of somebody weaker, which is the sense Alma 4:10 needs. The 1830 text prints 'stumbling block' as two words and 1920 hyphenated it — a change toward the KJV's own 'stumbling-block' at Ezekiel 3:20 (CONVENTIONS §8), though the sense is not Ezekiel's.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 8 is an argument that a believer's own liberty, exercised without regard for who is watching, destroys the weaker brother: 'shall not the conscience of him which is weak be emboldened' (8:10). Alma 4:10-11 is the same mechanism at the scale of a whole church — its wickedness a stumbling block to those outside it, its example leading unbelievers 'on from one piece of iniquity to another'. Read against Paul, the striking thing is what the Book of Mormon has changed: Paul's stumblingblock is a permitted thing done carelessly, Alma's is sin outright, and the transposition makes the borrowed figure heavier than its source. 1 Corinthians 10:32, 'Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God', is the same argument's summary and the machine's highest-ranked candidate three times over in this chapter.

4:10.note: 'The wickedness of the church was a great stumbling block to those who did not belong to the church.' The KJV word is used eleven times, but in only two of them does an insider's conduct become the obstacle for an outsider, and both are Paul on the Corinthian and Roman congregations. The next verse's 'example of the church began to lead those who were unbelievers, on from one piece of iniquity to another' repeats 1 Corinthians 8:10's emboldened conscience without repeating its words, which is why the row sits here and carries 8:10 as a composite rather than as a second link.

4:12.text: And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others:

provenance.other: “despised others” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “shall be abased” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 23:12, Luke 14:11 and Luke 18:14 — of which only Luke 18:14 stands in the same parable as the singleton.
provenance.significance: The two halves of Alma 4:12-13 are the two men of the parable. Luke 18:9 gives the first exactly — 'certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others' — and Luke 18:14 gives the antithesis on which the Book of Mormon's sentence is hinged, 'every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted': some lifting themselves up with their pride, despising others; while others were abasing themselves. What the borrowing does with its source is worth noticing. In Luke the exalting and the abasing are two individuals at prayer and the reversal is eschatological, God's to perform. In Alma they are two parties in a congregation and the abasing is voluntary and present, something the humble do to themselves in the same clause that has them succouring the poor. The parable has been converted from a warning about prayer into a description of a class division, and the borrowed verb changed voice on the way.

4:12.note: 'Some lifting themselves up with their pride, despising others' — against Luke 18:9's 'trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others', the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase. The next verse's 'abasing themselves' completes the pair from Luke 18:14. Two words and a structure, well below any quotation threshold; the case rests on the singleton and on the fact that the source supplies both sides of Alma's antithesis in the right order.

4:12.text: Then shall they also answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister unto thee?

provenance.other: “athirst” occurs in exactly five KJV verses; three are literal thirst or the invitation of Revelation, and only Matthew 25:44 places the word in a roll of the destitute beside the naked and the sick. The Book of Mormon's list — needy, naked, hungry, athirst, sick — has four of the six members of that roll, in a scrambled but recognisable order.
provenance.significance: Matthew 25 states the list twice, and Alma 4:12 has taken it from the wrong mouth. At 25:35-36 the sheep are told what they did: 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat; I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink.' The word 'athirst' belongs only to the second statement, 25:44, which is the goats' protest — 'when saw we thee an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister unto thee?' So the vocabulary in which Alma describes people turning their backs on the needy is the vocabulary of those who are told, at the judgment, that they turned their backs; and the very next verse, 4:13, supplies the sheep's side of the same list, imparting substance and feeding the hungry. The two verses are the two halves of Matthew 25, and the sorting has already happened before the chapter says a word about judgment.

4:12.note: 'Turning their backs upon the needy, and the naked, and those which were hungry, and those which were athirst, and those which were sick and afflicted.' The distinctive word is 'athirst', which in this sense the KJV uses once, in the goats' answer at Matthew 25:44. Alma 1:27 has the same roll on its positive side ('the poor, and the needy, and the sick, and the afflicted') and is the book's first use; the reason to write the row here rather than only cross-reference it is that Alma 4:12 adds 'athirst' and the turned backs, which is what pins the wording to the second of Matthew's two lists rather than the first.

4:13.text: Have I committed an offence in abasing myself that ye might be exalted, because I have preached to you the gospel of God freely?

provenance.other: “abasing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The finite forms are commoner — “shall be abased” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — so the participle is the only distinctive part of the contact.
provenance.significance: The KJV's single 'abasing' sits in the one Pauline sentence about a minister who lowered himself so that his hearers might be raised, and did it by preaching 'the gospel of God freely' — without charge. That is the practice this book has already made its test of a true teacher at Alma 1:26, and it is what Alma himself does at 4:18-20 when he keeps the priesthood and hands the judgment seat away. So the word arrives already attached to the chapter's own solution to the problem it is describing: against a church whose members are lifted up, the answer offered is a ministry that abases itself and takes nothing for it.

4:13.note: 'While others were abasing themselves, succoring those who stood in need of their succor.' The participle is a KJV singleton at 2 Corinthians 11:7, which is worth recording even though the primary source of the exalt/abase antithesis in these two verses is Luke 18:14 (linked at 4:12). The interest is that the one place the KJV inflects the verb this way is a passage about self-lowering ministry supported by nobody, which is where this chapter ends up six verses later.
4:13.whyNot: A single participle, and English inflection could produce it from Luke 18:14's 'abased' without any contact with 2 Corinthians at all. The senses also differ: Paul abases himself in the conduct of a mission, whereas Alma 4:13's humble abase themselves in devotion and almsgiving. Withdraw the row if the Lukan link at 4:12 is thought to account for the vocabulary on its own.

4:14.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,

provenance.other: “resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Alma 4:14 does not have the phrase entire; it has 'the resurrection of the dead' and 'deliverance of Jesus Christ from the bands of death' split across a clause boundary, with 'deliverance' standing where the KJV has 'resurrection' and 'the bands of death' where it has 'the dead'.
provenance.significance: If the contact is real it is a substitution rather than a borrowing, and the substituted words are the argument: Peter's resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead becomes a deliverance of Jesus Christ from the bands of death, which converts an event into a rescue and makes Christ the one delivered rather than only the one raised. The surrounding matter agrees: 1 Peter 1:3-8 has the hope that looks forward, the inheritance reserved, and a joy the believer has now in something not yet seen, all of which Alma 4:14 states in a single sentence — looking forward to that day, retaining a remission of sins, filled with great joy.

4:14.note: 'Because of the resurrection of the dead, according to the will, and power, and deliverance of Jesus Christ from the bands of death.' The n-gram stream sees only 'Jesus Christ from the'; what makes it worth a row is that the KJV joins those words to a resurrection exactly once, and that the joy-in-hope frame of 1 Peter 1:3-8 matches the rest of the verse. 'Bands of death' is in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own idiom, used heavily in the next chapter.
4:14.whyNot: Split agreement across a clause boundary with the head noun replaced, which is weak evidence on its own; 'the resurrection of the dead' occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses and is Pauline boilerplate, and 'Jesus Christ' beside it may be no more than the two commonest words in the register meeting by chance.

4:19.text: See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant.

provenance.other: “pull down” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Jeremiah 1:10, Jeremiah 18:7 and Luke 12:18 — and “pulling down” occurs in exactly one, 2 Corinthians 10:4. tools/mediation-check.py was run on the pair and returns one decisive point: the Book of Mormon has Jeremiah's infinitive 'pull down', not Paul's gerund 'pulling down'. The wording is therefore Jeremiah's even though the argument is Paul's.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 1:10 is a commission: a man set over nations and kingdoms 'to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant' — and set over them holding no office in any of them, which is exactly the position Alma has just put himself in by delivering the judgment seat to Nephihah and keeping only the word. What Alma pulls down is not a kingdom but 'all the pride and craftiness, and all the contentions', and the instrument is named twice in the verse: 'by the word of God'. That is where 2 Corinthians 10:4 presses, and it should be recorded even though the diff went the other way — 'the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds' is the doctrine of Alma 4:18-20 in one sentence, that the judgment seat was the carnal weapon and was laid down on purpose.
provenance.alternative: 2 Corinthians 10:4, on the argument rather than the wording; note that 1 Corinthians 3:3, the source at 4:9, is one of only three KJV settings for “not carnal” and 2 Corinthians 10:4 is another, so the chapter touches both ends of that small set.

4:19.note: 'That he might pull down, by the word of God, all the pride and craftiness, and all the contentions which was among his people.' Two candidates compete and they pull opposite ways: Jeremiah 1:10 has the verb form, 2 Corinthians 10:4 has the situation. mediation-check.py decides the wording for Jeremiah on the single point where the two diverge, and the row is filed accordingly with the Pauline reading kept as the alternative. 'Craftiness' is not decisive either way — it occurs in five KJV verses, two of them Pauline.
